title: At what point does "vibe coding" stop being game development and start being a custom commission ?
author: Aka_Athenes
selftext:
*I posted this as a comment in the thread "I didn't write a single line of this. Claude did. 60k units, in the browser, on a MacBook", but I thought it might be interesting to post it as a standalone thread.*  
  
One thing that leaves me puzzled about vibe coding is the way it changes our relationship with creation. I'm not making a value judgment here. I'm speaking from a personal and philosophical perspective.

As a developer, what has always brought me satisfaction was never just the final result. A large part of the appeal lies in the process itself: analyzing a problem, designing a solution, understanding constraints, making architectural decisions, fixing mistakes, and gradually seeing a system emerge whose components and trade-offs you fully understand.

Vibe coding tends to shift part of that experience. When AI directly produces most of the implementation, the user can obtain a functional result without having gone through the path that led to its construction. The result exists, but the relationship we have with it changes in nature. We are no longer necessarily building the object ourselves; we specify it, then receive it. Beyond a certain point, it may start to resemble a product more than a personal creation.

Of course, not all uses are equivalent. Someone who simply describes an objective and passively accepts the output is primarily acting as a consumer. On the other hand, someone who defines goals, evaluates proposals, makes trade-offs, rejects certain solutions, improves others, and guides the project over time is clearly participating in a creative process. However, their role becomes closer to that of a creative director, project manager, or client than that of a craftsman involved in every stage of the work.

Let's take a deliberately extreme example. If tomorrow it becomes possible to say :  
"Create a GTA-inspired game set in Berlin and southern Germany, featuring a newly arrived South Korean immigrant as the protagonist, with RPG progression systems inspired by The Division. Here's the story..."

and then receive a complete game after a few iterations, a question arises:

Did I create a video game, or did I simply commission a video game tailored exactly to my tastes ?  
This is why the question that interests me is not whether vibe coding is useful or efficient.

The real question is: at what point does the activity still primarily qualify as creation, and at what point does it become closer to placing a custom order or making a purchase?

I don't believe there is a universal answer. However, it seems obvious to me that for people who derive satisfaction from understanding mechanisms, solving problems, and progressively mastering complexity, part of the value of the activity lies precisely in what automation seeks to remove.

That, in my view, is the point worth discussing.

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
You're essentially asking the question "What is art and why do we care about it?"

Nobody's had a truly objective, definitive answer since the dawn of time.  AI doesn't change that, it's just another tool.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
It’s interesting as a non developer to watch developers wrestle with these questions. I have always had to rely on someone else to make my vision a reality on any meaningful scale. 

Just in this post you have gone through the role of designer and then of publisher. You are becoming a commissioner of content rather than the author. Developers are now having to struggle with the same questions and challenges that non-devs have had for years. How to keep the very clever, slightly unstable and occasionally stubborn code writers on track?

comments.author: Apalala__
comments.body:
None of that has any value to me. I just want my game to exist.  
How it should be framed is how AI can help you create your vision, not on Legitimacy.  
This is literally just easy mode and hard mode argument in a different coat.

comments.author: KreemPeynir
comments.body:
When you ask another human being to do, thats when it became a commision. 

You could argue the "AI do it all and therefore you didnt do it" but thats not a valid reason to deny authorship. 

If I use a game engine, instead of making one by myself, will a count as commission a game? Since the most hard part, the infrastructure, taken care of by game engine.

Better tools were keep coming and making devs less focus on the perfect code, and more focus on the idea they wanna execute.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
A game engine is different, it's just a collection of tools. 

Once AI is mostly hands off then you're not putting in any of the actual work, knowledge or skill required.

If you had an idea for an image and told an artist what you wanted and they made the image, you wouldn't say look at this image I created. You would say here's my idea brought to life by an artist.

Imo it's the same for AI, if you've done almost none of the work then yes it's your idea but it's created by AI so you are technically commissioning the AI to make your idea for you.

replies.author: KreemPeynir
replies.body:
You could argue the same thing with game engines. 

Most people who uses game engines dont know how to setup rendering with vulkan or opengl. 
Therefore they use less skill, knowlage and work conpared people who dont use one. 

If its the "minimum effort" requirement not meting with AI useage. I would like to know this "minimum requirment" as well.


A commision from an artist is commision, because its another human being. Unlike AI which is just a tool.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Using a game engine is nothing like asking AI to make a game for you.

AI is only a tool if it's used that way. I'm not talking about AI assisted games I'm talking about AI making your game for you. As AI improves that's going to become easier and easier for everyone. At the point you're just asking the AI to make a game for you, it's a commission because you're outsourcing all the work to AI.

replies.author: GigaTerra
replies.body:
>A game engine is different, it's just a collection of tools.

How is that different from an AI, and AI is just an collection of tools. In fact most modern AI applications like 3D AI models are less than 10% machine learning, and mostly Gaussian Splatting.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body: Making a game using a game engine and asking AI to make you a game are completely different. We're not talking about AI assisted. The OP was asking at what point does it become more like a commission. Which is at the point where AI is doing all the work for you. Then you're just the ideas guy.

replies.author: Warrmak
replies.body: There is no way to separate creative vision from the creative mechanism?  What about making a movie? Does the director not have creative control?

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Yes that's why they are called a director but they are not going to take credit for making the art, the sets, the acting etc.

Some directors are good artists too, people like James Cameron for example. They will be able give people such as concept artists much better direction with their own art but directors who are not are really just going to give the artists ideas or vibes, the actual final art is going to come mostly from the artists. Many concept artists for example are also chosen to work on movies because of their art.

Applying that to any creative process using AI and you're doing the same. If you don't know code and using AI for all your code then you are not programming, if you can't create art and are using AI to generate it you are not creating art. The AI is doing it for you. If you are relying on those things it's also highly likely that a lot of the ideas and creative decisions are being made by AI too.

As AI improves it's going to become easier and easier for people to basically prompt a game. So easy that a person will need no skills or knowledge whatsoever. Those people will not be game devs or artists, they will be people asking AI to make a game for them based loosely on an idea they had.

comments.author: recK7
comments.body: Does David Cage develop all the code for his games? Or is he the visionary / game director with many… agents… doing what he envisions? I like to think about AI that way.

comments.author: kazuyette
comments.body: With the advent of AI like Claude, I can now feel like Hideo Kojima producing my gaming and letting Claude do the heavy lifting.

replies.author: vreo
replies.body: Pretty much this. You become the strategist, the game designer, the visionary. AI makes you the chef of your own little army of artificial developers. As a sole developer your leverage is limited, with AI you can multiply yourself and become a director.

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
The difference between vibe coding and commission is simple, **responsibility**.

If you commission someone to do something it is their responsibility to deliver an working product as specified. They will ask you questions and try to understand what it is you want, they take half of the responsibility.

With vibe coding the programmer takes 100% of the responsibility, the AI is not going to ask you questions, it is not going to clarify, it is not going to try and understand because it can't. It will simply do as told, and it is your fault if it wasn't what you wanted.

comments.author: Warrmak
comments.body: What would you consider Todd Howard?  Does he not exercise creative control over his visions? Does the mechanism of creation make one more legitimate than another?

comments.author: Warrmak
comments.body: Who was the creative mind behind Pulp Fiction?  The Matrix?  The Big Lebowski?
